title: Pressure systems, electrical & equipment safety
blurb: PUWER, the Pressure Systems Safety Regulations for compressors and autoclaves, electrical safety and PAT, and what to do with faulty kit.
question: While setting up, you notice the cable on a portable curing light charger is frayed near the plug. Later the compressor starts making an unusual banging noise, and the autoclave door seal looks worn. Which laws cover this equipment, and what should you do about each problem?

teach.h: Safe equipment is a legal requirement
teach.body: Everything you use at work, from the dental chair to the ultrasonic bath, is 'work equipment'. The Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998 (PUWER) require it to be suitable for its purpose, maintained in a safe condition, inspected where needed, and used only by people who have had the right information and training. Some equipment has extra laws of its own because of the particular danger it carries: stored pressure, electricity, lifting, or radiation.

teach.caption: LOLER only matters if the practice has lifting equipment such as a hoist or lift. Equipment for lifting people needs a thorough examination at least every 6 months.

teach.body: A compressor and a steam steriliser (autoclave) both hold energy under pressure. If one fails, it can burst violently. The Pressure Systems Safety Regulations 2000 require: a written scheme of examination drawn up by a competent person; periodic examinations by a competent person (often an engineer from the insurer); proper maintenance; trained operators; and records kept. These sit alongside the daily and weekly autoclave tests in HTM 01-05.

teach.caption: User checks include the autoclave's daily automatic control test, looking at door seals, and draining the compressor as the manufacturer instructs.

teach.body: The Electricity at Work Regulations 1989 require electrical systems and equipment to be maintained so they don't cause danger. Portable appliance testing (PAT) by a competent person is a common way of showing this. The law sets no fixed PAT interval: how often depends on a risk assessment of the type of equipment and how it is used. Between tests, users do a quick visual check before use: plug, cable, casing, and any scorch marks.

steps.label: Isolate it
steps.sub: Switch off and unplug, if safe

items.label: Oxidising
items.sub: Oxygen: keep from grease and heat

teach.body: Dental equipment such as curing lights, handpieces and autoclaves are medical devices. If a device fault harms someone, or could have done, it should be reported to the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) through the Yellow Card scheme, as well as to the manufacturer. Always follow the manufacturer's instructions for use, and don't use new equipment until you've been trained on it.

teach.text: A frayed or damaged cable is NEVER fixed with insulating tape and put back into use. Take it out of service, label it, and report it.

items: PUWER 1998: equipment suitable, maintained, inspected, and users trained.
Pressure Systems Safety Regs 2000: compressors and autoclaves need a written scheme of examination and competent-person inspections.
Electricity at Work Regs 1989: keep electrics safe. PAT frequency is set by risk assessment.
Faulty kit: stop, isolate, label, report, record, repair.
LOLER only if you have lifting equipment; IRR17 for X-ray units; MHRA Yellow Card for device incidents.

summary: You can now match dental equipment to the law that covers it, explain how compressors and autoclaves are kept safe under the Pressure Systems Safety Regulations, describe electrical safety and PAT, and deal correctly with faulty equipment.

A.q: You notice damaged insulation on the lead of a portable light. What is the best response?
options: Wrap insulating tape round it and continue
Use it carefully until the end of the day
Remove it from use and report it
Use it only when no patients are present
A.why: Damaged electrical equipment must be taken out of use straight away, labelled and reported.

whyNot.0: Taping over damage hides the fault and leaves an electrical hazard.
whyNot.1: Any further use risks shock or fire.
whyNot.3: Staff can still be hurt when patients aren't present.

A.q: Which regulations apply specifically to the practice's compressor and autoclave?
options: The Lifting Operations and Lifting Equipment Regulations 1998
The Control of Substances Hazardous to Health Regulations 2002
A.why: Compressors and steam sterilisers contain stored pressure, so they fall under the Pressure Systems Safety Regulations 2000.

whyNot.1: Manual handling regulations cover lifting and carrying loads.
whyNot.2: LOLER covers lifting equipment such as hoists.

A.q: How often must portable electrical appliances be PAT tested by law?
A.why: The law requires electrical equipment to be maintained safely but sets no fixed PAT interval; frequency depends on risk.

whyNot.0: Six months is not a legal requirement for PAT.
whyNot.1: Annual testing is a common choice, but it isn't fixed in law.
whyNot.2: Three years may suit some low-risk items, but it isn't a legal rule.

B.q: Under the Pressure Systems Safety Regulations, what must be in place for an autoclave?
options: A COSHH assessment of the steam
B.why: A written scheme of examination, drawn up by a competent person, sets out how and when the pressure system is examined.

whyNot.0: Steam isn't assessed under COSHH; the pressure risk is the issue.
whyNot.2: RIDDOR is for reporting incidents, not routine compliance.
whyNot.3: LOLER covers lifting equipment, not autoclaves.

B.q: Which law requires work equipment to be suitable, maintained and used only by trained staff?
B.why: The Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998 set general duties for all work equipment.

whyNot.1: HTM 07-01 is guidance on healthcare waste.

B.q: A handpiece fault burns a patient's lip. Besides the manufacturer, who should the incident be reported to?
B.why: Adverse incidents involving medical devices are reported to the MHRA through the Yellow Card scheme.

whyNot.1: CQC may need to know about serious incidents, but device faults go to the MHRA.
whyNot.2: The fire service deals with fire safety.

C.q: What is the correct FIRST action on finding a faulty piece of equipment?
C.why: Stop using it first, then isolate, label, report and record.

whyNot.0: Recording comes after it has been made safe.
whyNot.1: Replacement is decided later by the manager.
whyNot.3: Repairs must be carried out by a competent person.

C.q: Which of these is the main hazard that the Pressure Systems Safety Regulations aim to prevent?
C.why: Stored pressure can be released violently if a vessel fails, causing serious injury.

whyNot.0: Steam burns are a risk, but the regulations focus on the release of stored energy.
whyNot.1: Noise is a separate workplace hazard.
whyNot.2: Infection control is covered by HTM 01-05.

C.q: When would LOLER 1998 most likely apply in a dental practice?
options: When the practice has a patient hoist
C.why: LOLER covers lifting equipment, such as patient hoists and passenger lifts.

whyNot.1: Autoclaves fall under the Pressure Systems Safety Regulations.
whyNot.3: PAT relates to the Electricity at Work Regulations.

reteach.title: Think MOT for your equipment
reteach.question: A car needs an MOT, servicing and a driver who knows how to drive it. How does that map to the equipment in a dental practice?

blocks.body: PUWER is the general rule that the car must be roadworthy and the driver trained. The compressor and autoclave are like a car with a pressurised tank: they need a special inspection plan (the written scheme) and a qualified examiner. Electrical items get their own safety check (PAT). And before every journey you walk round the car: that's your quick visual check of plugs and cables. If a tyre is flat, you don't drive it: you take it off the road and get it fixed.

explain.body: All work equipment must be suitable, maintained in a safe condition, inspected where needed, and used only by trained people who have the information they need.

test.q: A new ultrasonic bath is delivered. Under PUWER, what must happen before staff use it?
options: It must be PAT tested by the user
It must be reported under RIDDOR
It must be registered with HSE
Staff must be trained to use it
test.why: PUWER requires users to have adequate information and training before using work equipment.

whyNot.0: PAT is done by a competent person, and new equipment doesn't need an immediate test.

explain.body: Compressors and autoclaves need a written scheme of examination, periodic examination by a competent person, maintenance, trained users and records, under the Pressure Systems Safety Regulations 2000.

test.q: Who draws up the written scheme of examination for a compressor?
test.why: The regulations require the written scheme to be drawn up or certified by a competent person.

whyNot.0: Reception staff aren't qualified to do this.
whyNot.1: Nurses do user checks, not the scheme.
whyNot.3: CQC inspects practices; it doesn't write examination schemes.

explain.body: Electrics must be maintained to prevent danger. PAT is done by a competent person at intervals set by risk. Users check plugs, cables and casings before use and report damage.

test.q: During your visual check, which finding means an appliance must be taken out of use?
options: A PAT label from last year
A slightly warm casing in use
A cable tidied with a clip
test.why: Scorch marks suggest overheating or a fault, so the appliance must be withdrawn and reported.

whyNot.0: A recent PAT label is a good sign, not a fault.
whyNot.2: Many devices get slightly warm in normal use.
whyNot.3: A tidy cable clip is good practice.

explain.body: Stop using it, isolate it if safe, label it 'do not use', report it, record it, and leave repairs to a competent person. Report device incidents to the MHRA through Yellow Card.

test.q: Why should faulty equipment be clearly labelled 'do not use'?
options: To stop someone else using it
So the engineer can find it
To show it has been PAT tested
test.why: A clear label stops colleagues picking up and using equipment that isn't safe.

whyNot.1: Helpful, but not the main safety reason.
whyNot.2: The label is a practical safety step, not an MHRA labelling requirement.
whyNot.3: A fault label is the opposite of a pass label.
